$comment: Per-checker configuration for this repo. Each checker falls back to its own defaults when its key is absent, so deleting a block degrades to the built-in behaviour rather than to an empty scope. What lives here is what changes between repos: layout, thresholds, and the regexes that name one stack's idioms. What stays in code is the rule itself.
$profile: The shape this repo claims to hold, not the tools it uses: baseline = one axis measures · standard = two axes block, both meta-checks present · hardened = every declared axis blocks and every gate job is asserted. A profile is a claim someone else can fail you on, which is the only kind worth writing down.
$baselines: Level 2 means `baseline the old, block the new`, so an axis at 2 must name WHERE its debt is frozen and WHICH direction counts as improvement — otherwise the frozen number is a photograph nobody can compare against. `improves`: down = a per-key number may only decrease · shrink = a set may only lose members · tighten = a status may only move to the stricter value. The direction lives here rather than inside the baseline file because `--update-baseline` rewrites those files, and a rule that a re-freeze can silently drop is not a rule.

form.owns: file & function length; whitespace, import order, recommended rules; where an integration provider's name may be written, and whether every provider's declaration carries the fields the generic paths read

knowledge.gate: check-honest-costs + check-injected-doc-modes + check-pat-surface + check-status-tuples + check-doc-citations + build-flow-map
knowledge.owns: whether a document asking to be adopted prices what adopting it costs; whether a doc injected into every session names the pipeline mode its status transitions belong to; whether the PAT permission menu covers every route it claims; whether one question in the source has more than one answer; whether a document's citations of this repo's own files are still true; whether the flow map is generated rather than hand-kept

relations.owns: which module may depend on which

alsoBaseline.$why: archmap lock writes this, and without a direction that command is an amnesty button: run it and today's violations stop blocking. `down` means the frozen TOTAL may not rise and no per-key count may rise, so freezing a new file in fails and letting a blob grow inside its own entry fails, while fixing one and re-freezing is free.

behaviour.owns: whether a test asserts behaviour or restates a declaration; whether the integration suite enters the function every declared flow step sits on; whether every tracked test file is collected by a runner at all

record.owns: whether the external record of what shipped keeps the heading its readers parse for, whether an entry once published can be removed without saying so, and whether a NEW entry stays inside the word budget a reader can actually read
record.$why: The other five axes each own a property of the CODE. On 2026-08-28 commit 3df9a8e9 removed 1,034 lines from CHANGELOG.md inside a docs-pointer commit whose message never named the file; twelve gates ran and every one passed, because the record was nobody's. No baseline: it starts at zero debt, and a removal is declared per-instance in .forge/changelog-amnesty.json rather than frozen in bulk — a public record is edited one line at a time or not at all. Budget added 2026-09-16 (ENTRY_WORD_BUDGET, 40): unbounded, the record reached 443 entries and 86,206 words with a median of 173 — the second failure mode, opposite the raw-commit dump, where the detail is present but not findable. It measures only entries a change ADDS, for the same reason there is no baseline: the entries already published are rewritten one at a time, not frozen by declaring them once.

comment.owns: what a comment SAYS: density against the code around it, the length of one run, historical narration, and one comment restating another. The rules are eslint-plugin-code-quality's, vendored at .forge/code-quality and enabled in eslint.config.mjs; this axis is the baseline ESLint has no concept of.
comment.$why: The codemap checker that used to own comment content was deleted with its annotations, which left prose in this repo measured by nothing. The plugin replacing it ran as `pnpm lint:code-quality` and sat in no row of verify, no job of ci-passed and no axis here — written and unmeasured, which is the failure this whole design exists to prevent (ISS-1111).
comment.$amnesty: 73 findings across 67 files are frozen on 2026-09-21 at the head this branch lands at: 63 comment-density, 5 no-duplicate-comment, 4 no-historical-narration, 1 max-consecutive-comment-lines. It was 54 across 51 files when first frozen at bd2e36d5e on 2026-09-20; the extra 19 findings in 16 files are the merged deliverables of the 26 commits that landed on main while ISS-1105/ISS-1111 sat on_hold waiting for ISS-1123, and they are amnestied rather than paid because ISS-1111 scopes out lowering any existing count and because paying them means editing other issues' landed work. What it costs: those 67 files keep comments a reader was told to delete, nothing dates them, and 19 of them were written after this gate was designed and before it could land — that is the price of a gate held. `original` stays 54 and is never raised by a re-freeze, so every run prints the growth as a negative drain (today: -35%) rather than hiding it behind a new starting number. Freezing was the price of the gate landing green rather than red on work nobody had scheduled. It ends when the measured count in .forge/comment-baseline.json reaches 0 and this axis goes to level 3. The gate does NOT cover the other halves of `pnpm lint:code-quality` — raw elements, pass-through wrappers, crowded directories and the design-token sweep — which belong to axes nobody has declared and would have imported roughly 5,400 unjudged findings into this one.

archmap.$comment: Ceiling on edges `arch check` cannot resolve. Measured 2026-08-23: 171, all of them node_modules subpath exports (hono/http-exception and friends), which belong to no module and so cannot violate a contract. It was 997 until `.arch.json` declared a tsConfig — 841 of those were web-v2's `@/*` alias, and an unresolvable edge is DROPPED, so three locked contracts over that package were being checked against an empty graph. It had drifted back to 201 by 2026-09-16, 167 of them `hono/http-exception`; a `hono/*` entry in `.arch-tsconfig.json` took it to 33 with `archmap check` still reporting 0 blocking and the same 10 frozen, so nothing was being hidden by the drop. The ceiling came down 200 -> 50 in the same change (ISS-1046): a ceiling four times the measurement is not a ratchet. What remains is the MCP SDK's subpath exports and mermaid. Audit rule R7 fails if it climbs back.

status-tuples.$comment: ISS-1106 — one question, one answer. Two constants holding the same status tuple are one answer with two labels whatever they are called, and an inline copy is a third label with no name at all; each is a place a later change can move one copy and leave the rest. Measured on main at bd2e36d5e: 8 tuples declared more than once, 13 inline restatements, and `['closed','dropped']` under four separate names. The three vocabularies are read out of `packages/core/src/db/schema.ts` rather than listed here, so a rename there stops the scan instead of quietly narrowing it. What it deliberately does not read, each stated at the point it is skipped: SQL string literals (ISS-1109 and ISS-1110 own those), test files, type unions, and a tuple written as an object-literal value, which is a table row rather than a named question. A pair that must differ is admitted by a `status-tuple: differs — <reason>` comment at the declaration, so the reason sits where a reader of the constant will find it rather than in this file. ISS-1106 criterion 13: `packages/web-v2/src` is scanned too, because a browser file answering `a job is live` a second time is the same defect as a core file doing it — `features/pipeline/activity.ts` held the four job statuses under `OPEN_STATUSES` while the gate read green. Widening the roots alone found nothing: web-v2 is written with double quotes and the literal matcher read single only, so 1648 files scanned and 0 extra tuples. Both halves are the fix. There is no web-v2 exclusion and no amnesty: the answers that were genuinely restated moved into `@forge/contracts/status-sets`, which web-v2 imports and `packages/core/src/db/status-sets-parity.test.ts` binds to core member for member, and the two whose tuples only coincide — the transition menu's discard group and the Finished filter cut — carry the `differs` reason at their own declaration. The limit this widening exposed, stated so the next reader does not have to find it: a gate that keys a tuple by its members is blind to a copy that has already DRIFTED. The browser's blocked chip answered `is this blocker settled?` with `['awaiting_release','closed']` while core answers it with `BLOCKER_SETTLED_STATUSES` = `['developed','testing','awaiting_release','closed']`, so the two never collided and the gate said nothing while the screen told people work was held that Forge would dispatch. It took a reader, not this checker. This checker catches a copy BEFORE it rots and never after, which is what makes the parity test in `packages/core/src/db/status-sets-parity.test.ts` the other half rather than a belt on a brace: the gate stops a second declaration appearing, and the parity test stops an existing pair drifting apart. ISS-1106 criterion 13, second pass: at the merged head the identifier `LIVE_JOB_STATUSES` meant four statuses in `jobs/status-sets.ts` and three in `pipeline/runs-rollup.ts`, where a `Record<JobStatus, boolean>` classified the vocabulary a second time and fed the panel's `live_jobs` count — and the gate read green through TWO holes at once. The literal matcher does not read a record, and the `status-tuple: differs` marker on `UNHELD_LIVE_JOB_STATUSES`, which is about a DIFFERENT tuple, was being read as a blanket excuse that let a second declaration of the unheld set stand. Both are closed: a `Record<…Status, boolean>` is now a declaration of its `true` keys, and a marker excuses a declaration only against a peer it names. A third rule landed with them, because the first two were not enough: one NAME answers one question. Without it the planted `LIVE_JOB_STATUSES` under a three-member value still passed — the marker on `UNHELD_LIVE_JOB_STATUSES` names `LIVE_JOB_STATUSES`, so a rogue declaration wearing that name satisfied the peer check and left one unexcused answer in the group. A name holding two tuples is now refused whatever the markers say, which is the only rule of the three that would have caught the defect by its own spelling rather than by its value. `Record<…Status, T>` for any other T stays unread on purpose — grouping a lookup table's keys by value invents questions nobody asked (`contracts/issue-vocabulary.ts`'s `KERNEL_TO_LABEL` would answer "a person is owed something"). Test files are scanned now, but only for `.each` case lists: that list is the domain a test claims to cover, so a member added to a constant leaves it silently covering less, while every other tuple in a test file is the assertion itself and importing the constant would make it vacuous. The condition that ends that narrowing is a rule that can tell an expectation from a domain. Two things this pass found and did NOT take: `pipelineRunStatuses` is still not one of the vocabularies read, so `['completed','failed','cancelled']` and `['paused','running']` are attributed to `agentSessionStatuses` or to nothing — adding it surfaces eleven inline restatements of `LIVE_PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES` plus a second `LIVE_RUN_STATUSES` in web-v2, which is a collapse of its own and is written up in docs/proposals/status-tuple-residuals.md rather than ridden in here. One piece of that collapse DID land, because it cost two lines and the module-owns-the-concept rule is this issue's own: `LIVE_PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES` moved from `issues/issue-lease.ts`, which had one caller, into the new `pipeline/status-sets.ts` beside `TERMINAL_PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES`. Neither is visible to this checker — `['running','paused']` fits no vocabulary it reads and `['completed','failed','cancelled']` is attributed to `agentSessionStatuses` — so the move is for the reader, and the eleven inline copies stay where the proposal left them.

doc-citations.$comment: ISS-1112 — a document that names a file makes a claim a machine can check, and nothing checked it: 93 documents had drifted far enough to be deleted rather than corrected before this landed, one of them crediting an invariant to a test file not in the tree. The unit is a CITATION, never a document — prose is not checkable and this does not try. A citation is resolved in two scopes and no third — the document's own directory and the package the document sits in — with a path written from the repository root resolved exactly or not at all. Nothing falls back to the whole tree, and no part of resolution reads whether the target is present: a resolution that widens at the moment a file disappears is a resolution that cannot report the disappearance. The cost is real and is paid rather than hidden: a document at the repository root writes the full path or is told it cites nothing, which is what the sweep in ISS-1112 did to sixteen citations in `CLAUDE.md` and `scripts/README.md`. One residual is stated at `scripts/check-doc-citations.mjs` rather than left to be found: a document inside a scope citing a root-level file whose name is ALSO taken inside that scope resolves to the root copy while it exists and to the scoped namesake once it is deleted. Closing it takes a syntactic root notation and a rewrite of every rooted citation in the repository. Nothing detects the collision while both files exist either, because the exact match returns before any scoped candidate is looked for; what bounds it is only that it needs one name taken twice, at the root and inside the citing document's own scope, which this repository does not do today. Three shapes fail: a path no tracked file carries, a line-number citation (which CLAUDE.md already forbids by name), and a file.ts:symbol anchor whose file does not hold that symbol. One shape only reports: a citation whose target was changed after the document was, which is the still-true/edited/deleted worklist entry and not a build failure. What it cannot see, each stated where it is skipped: prose, fenced and indented code blocks, a path in another repository (which carries no extension here and so is not read as a citation at all), a symbol that still exists but has changed meaning, and whether a count or a number in a document is right. A token that is not a claim about this repository says so at the citation, in an HTML comment reading `doc-citation: unchecked `<token>` `<token>` — <why>`, which NAMES what it excuses: a window alone would reach every citation in the same paragraph, and the migration README's template marker sat three lines above a live `meta/_journal.json` it would then have hidden. A marker naming no token is refused rather than left to excuse nothing in silence. Resolution reads the working tree as well as the index, because `git ls-files` still lists a file deleted and not yet staged — which is the one run whose job is to notice it went.

skipDocs.why: The external record of what shipped. It records what was true on the day it shipped and is MEANT to age — a citation in a released entry going stale is the record working, not rotting. Named out of scope by ISS-1112 and owned by the `record` axis instead.

A proposal names the tree it WANTS, not the tree there is, so a forward reference and a dead citation are the same text and this checker cannot tell them apart. `check-honest-costs` already owns these documents on the axis they can be measured on: whether they price what adopting them costs.
A vendored third-party plugin's own documents, shipped with its source. Its citations are about its own tree and land here only because `pnpm install` needs no path outside the repo.
The same: `eslint-plugin-code-quality` vendored at a path inside the repo so installation needs no path outside it. Its documents are its author's.

Snapshots kept for recovery. A citation in a backup describes the tree AT THE TIME IT WAS TAKEN, which is the whole point of keeping it, so measuring it against today's tree would report the backup working as a fault.

provider-literals.$comment: ISS-1071 — an integration provider's name is written in the places that describe a provider, and nowhere else. The rule is about LOCATION, not about the value: `IntegrationProvider` makes 'coolify' legal everywhere the union is in scope, which is what a union is for, so no type can hold this and the check has to be a scan. What it matches, and the two bounds it carries, are stated at the top of scripts/lib/provider-literals.mjs.

unscannable.why: 'agent' is a provider name AND this repo's word for an actor, an author, a principal and a conversation participant — `kind: 'agent'`, `author: 'agent'`, `role: 'agent'`. Measured 2026-09-17 across the three scan roots: 81 files write the bare literal and at most six of them are about the integration, so including it would run the checker at over 90% noise, which is the one failure a checker cannot recover from — a reader who learns to skip the report also skips the real finding underneath it. What holds `agent` instead is the type (it is a member of IntegrationProvider, so a wrong use in an integration position is a compile error) plus the registry test that refuses the union and the registry when they disagree. Retire this entry when the actor vocabulary stops sharing the word, not before; the checker prints it on every run so the exclusion cannot go quiet.

allowed.why: The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT coolify and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT postman and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT epodsystem and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT sentry and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT rocketchat and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT github and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT google and no generic path reads it.
The registry itself. Every generic path asks a question here instead of naming a provider, which is precisely what makes this the file the names arrive in.

The `IntegrationProvider` union and `INTEGRATION_PROVIDERS` beside it are the vocabulary. The checker reads its own scanned set out of this file, so forbidding the names here would forbid the list it works from.

The database schema's own vocabulary. A column declared `{ enum: [...] }` stores these strings and rows already written carry them, so a name here is on disk in every deployment rather than a branch in code — `schema-conversations.ts` and `schema-rocketchat.ts` also name a provider in a TABLE name, which no refactor can reach without a migration.

The cross-package contract surface web-v2 reads. Core's production image does not carry contracts, so a runtime value cannot cross from core to here; where a provider name has to be legible on the web side it is written in contracts and held in lockstep by a parity test.

`DEPLOY_CAPABLE_PROVIDERS` — the list deliberately mirrored across the package boundary, because neither package may import a runtime value from the other. `integrations/deploy-capability-parity.test.ts` is the whole of what makes the second copy safe.

The web side's per-provider modules — the browser mirror of a provider's own directory. `providers/<provider>/section.tsx` is ABOUT that provider and no generic screen reads it; what is left in features/integrations/components and in derive.ts is generic and still reported.

`github` and `google` here are LOGIN identity providers — a different namespace that happens to share two words with the integration vocabulary. `providers.ts` answers /api/auth/oauth/providers, which never touches an integration binding, so a registry lookup here would be the wrong answer rather than a tidier one.

The browser half of the same login-identity namespace: the sign-in buttons and the token screens read `github`/`google` as OAuth providers, which is a different thing from an integration adapter that happens to share the word.

`'github'` here is `issues.source`, whose enum is `['manual','github']` (db/schema.ts, `issueSources`) — the issue-INTAKE vocabulary, not the integration-provider one. Same word, different column: every literal in this file is a value compared against `issues.source`, and the registry knows nothing about it.

`source: 'rocketchat'` here is a CONVERSATION source — the `conversations.source` vocabulary in db/schema-conversations.ts, beside 'web', 'widget' and 'telegram' — not the integration provider. Same word, different column, and this is a bench fixture describing where an utterance arrived from.

The `ConversationAdapter` union: which surface a conversation happened on. It mirrors the `conversations.source` column, not `integration_bindings.provider`, and it carries 'web' and 'widget' which are not integrations at all.

`<Icon name="github" />` is an icon in the design system's icon set, labelling `project.repoPath`. It names a glyph, not a provider — the card renders no integration binding and would render this mark for a repository hosted anywhere.

The one hand-built card, keyed 'github', is derived from `projects.repoPath` and NOT from any integration binding — which is exactly why `githubIntegration` declares `presentation: null`, so the registry loop cannot emit a second card that collides with it. Every other card in this file comes from a declaration.

An MCP tool module dedicated to one provider, sitting in `mcp/tools/` because that is where the MCP server discovers its `forge-*.ts` tools — the directory is the server's convention, not a generic path. The tool exists only to answer questions about epodsystem; no other provider's request reaches it.

The Coolify release path, named for the provider in the file name because the whole module is that provider's deploy dispatch. `release-batch/plan.ts` no longer decides WHETHER to use it by naming coolify — that is `declaration.releaseStep` now — so nothing generic reads this file to learn a provider exists.

Resolves the GitHub App installation credential a runner presents. Both literals filter `integration_bindings.provider` to find that App's binding, and the registry cannot answer 'which provider is the GitHub App' without naming it. The module is github's by name and purpose; it holds no branch that would have to grow a case when a provider is added.

integration-declarations.$comment: ISS-1071 — the registry is only a single door while every declaration behind it answers the questions the generic paths ask. A missing field does not fail to compile once a declaration reaches the registry through a widened type, and the reader then sees a provider that is inert rather than one that did not answer; five of seven adapters reached the old registry through `as any`. This walks the LIVE registry rather than the source, so the thing measured is what the process would hold at boot. `entrypoint` is imported under tsx with a synthetic env; its absence is exit 2, never a pass over an empty registry.

lint-budget.$comment: Registering a class is this list plus one `--update-baseline` run — no second script, no second baseline file. That is the whole claim ISS-833 made for a shared ratchet, and `packages/core` is the proof of it: its `warn`-severity rules produced 280 diagnostics that nothing counted, because biome exits 0 on a warning. A scope with no `drain` block is freeze-only.
lint-budget.$drain: Freezing does not reduce — the codemap baseline sat frozen for months at 3% drained. `drain` adds the rule that does: a file in the branch delta matching `include` and not `exclude`, whose baseline count is above zero, must come back STRICTLY lower. web-v2 declares none on purpose: 98 debt-carrying files with the formatter deliberately off is a separate decision from turning the linter on.

flows.name: dispatch
flows.description: An issue status change reaching a runner: apply-transition commits, a DB trigger writes the outbox row in the same transaction, the outbox worker re-emits it on the hooks bus, a subscriber fires a coalesced per-project sweep, the gates pick a job, the dispatcher hands it to a runner.

flows.name: release
flows.description: An issue reaching released and ending closed: merging the pull request IS the stamp — one operation writes merged_at, merged_commit_sha and the projection row, releasing every blocks dependent — the orchestrator enqueues the release job, the agent's close stamps merged_at as an assertion if it is still null, closing the run reaps the child jobs, and job completion dispatches the deploy.
